Dotenv Exposure Checker

Paste your site's URL. This sends a plain GET request to five well-known dotenv filenames (.env, .env.local, .env.production, .env.production.local, .env.development.local) and verifies each response against the real KEY=VALUE line shape of a dotenv file — not just an HTTP status — before calling anything exposed. Variable values are never read, stored, or shown anywhere by this tool — only variable names. See why .env files end up in production for the common causes and the fix for each. Only run this against a site you own or are authorised to test.

Run the check

Enter a site URL, then click Check.

Report

Every path checked

PathResult

Prefer a CLI, or hit a CORS wall in the browser?

Most servers don't send permissive CORS headers on arbitrary static paths, so a browser tab often cannot read a cross-origin response at all — you'll see a generic network error with no HTTP status. The CLI has no such restriction and is the one path guaranteed to complete: 

node check.mjs https://example.com/ --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if any path is exposed, so you can gate a deploy on it.

Common questions

Why would a production site be serving its own .env file?

Usually because a deploy step copies the whole project directory — .env included — to the web root instead of only the built output, or because a framework's static file server was pointed at the project root rather than a dedicated public/ directory. Node.js, Next.js, Laravel, Django, and Rails all read a project-root .env file by convention, so it commonly sits right next to the code the web server is meant to serve.

Does this tool show me the actual secret values?

No, never. This tool reads a response body only to check its line shape (is this KEY=VALUE formatted, like a real dotenv file) and to extract variable names — it never displays, stores, or reports a value, not even a redacted or partial one. A variable name like STRIPE_SECRET_KEY being present is already enough to know a real credential is likely exposed, without this tool ever needing to show what that credential is.

How is this different from just typing the URL into my browser?

A browser tab shows you the raw response, but many servers return their normal 200 page (a single-page app's fallback route, a themed 404) for literally any path — which can look plausible enough to misread as an exposure, or a real one might be dismissed without checking the content. This tool verifies the body actually has the real KEY=VALUE line shape of a dotenv file before calling anything exposed, and checks five well-known filenames in one run instead of one at a time. See how this compares to checking by hand.

Is it safe to point this at a URL?

This tool sends only ordinary GET requests to the five paths under the URL you name — the same requests your own browser already makes when you type one of those URLs in by hand — and it never writes or submits anything. It does not upload the URL or anything it finds to our servers when run in the browser; every request goes straight from your browser to the target. Still, only run this against a site you own or are authorised to test, the same caution you'd apply to any request tool aimed at someone else's server.

Does a clean report mean my deployment has no secrets exposed anywhere?

It means the five paths this run checked either returned a clean 401/403/404 or did not match the dotenv file shape expected for them. It does not check other common secret-exposure paths (a stray .git directory, a config.json, a backup archive), does not crawl the rest of the site, and only checks the one base URL you give it. Treat a clean report as evidence about what this run actually found, not a full audit of the deployment.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks five well-known paths with one GET request each. It never writes, submits, or modifies anything, never reads, stores, or shows a variable's value (only its name), does not check other common secret-exposure paths (a stray .git directory, a config.json, a backup archive), and cannot see an exposure at a path it never checked. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the site has no exposure.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every request goes straight from your browser to the URL you name — never through this site, and never logged or stored by us. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day — no site URLs, no file contents, no variable names or values, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. vs-checking-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the Dotenv Exposure Checker

Dotenv Exposure Checker vs. checking by hand

Typing yoursite.com/.env into a browser tab is a real, fast way to spot the single obvious case: a plainly readable file full of KEY=VALUE lines. It is also the method most developers already reach for first, and it genuinely works for that case.

CheckTyping the URL by handThis tool
Obvious plainly-readable .env fileCatches itCatches it
A server that returns 200 with a generic page for any path (soft-404)Can look plausible enough to misread either wayVerified against the real KEY=VALUE line shape before calling anything exposed
Checking all five common dotenv filenames, not just oneManual, easy to stop after trying the bare .envChecks .env, .env.local, .env.production, .env.production.local, and .env.development.local every run
Telling a live credential apart from an innocuous settingEasy to skim past in a wall of variable namesFlags a variable NAME that matches a common secret pattern (SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD, API_KEY) at a higher severity
Repeatable in CI on every deployManual, point-in-timeCLI returns a real exit code

When to still just look

If you only need a one-off sanity check on a URL you're already typing into the address bar, looking is fine — it's free and you're already there. The gap this tool closes is coverage and confidence: all five relevant filenames, not just the one you thought to try, each verified against the real file shape rather than eyeballed, every time a deploy happens, with an exit code a CI pipeline can act on.

Common questions

What does typing the URL into a browser tab actually show you?

Typing yoursite.com/.env into a browser tab is a fast, real check for the single obvious case: a plainly readable file full of KEY=VALUE lines. If that's what comes back, you don't need a tool to tell you it's exposed -- though you may not notice which of the lines is actually a live credential versus an innocuous setting.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Three ways this scripted check catches and a quick manual look easily misses: (1) a server that returns its normal 200 page (a single-page app's fallback route, a themed 404) for literally any path -- glancing at a response that looks like plausible text can be misread either way without checking its actual line shape. (2) Checking only the bare .env and not the four other common filenames (.env.local, .env.production, .env.production.local, .env.development.local) that frameworks like Next.js define and that often carry the developer's own real secrets rather than committed defaults. (3) A page full of variable names is easy to skim past without noticing which ones look like a real credential -- this tool names them explicitly by pattern (SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD, API_KEY, and similar) as a separate, higher severity.

Why does this matter for CI, not just a one-time check?

A manual check is a point-in-time look. A new deploy script, a server migration, or a CDN configuration change can reintroduce this exposure at any point after the last time someone happened to check. The CLI here returns a real exit code, so it can gate a deploy the same way a linter or test suite does -- catching a regression the day it ships rather than the next time someone thinks to check by hand.

why-env-files-end-up-in-production.html.text:
← Back to the Dotenv Exposure Checker

Why .env files end up in production

A dotenv file only becomes a problem when a production deployment leaves it publicly reachable. There are four common, independent ways that happens, and each has its own fix — fixing one does not fix the others.

1. The web root is the same directory .env lives in

Frameworks that read a project-root .env by convention (Node.js via dotenv, Next.js, Laravel, Django, Rails) expect it to sit beside the application code — not inside whatever directory the web server serves as static files. If the web server's document root is the project root itself, .env is servable like any other file. 

# Wrong: the web server's document root is the project root
document_root: /var/www/myapp/          # myapp/.env is right there, servable

# Right: serve only the build output, one level below
document_root: /var/www/myapp/dist/     # myapp/.env is outside the served tree entirely

2. A deploy script copies the whole project directory

Even with a separate web root in mind, a cp -r . or rsync -a ./ deploy script copies everything in the working directory — .env included — to wherever it is pointed. Copy only the built output, or exclude it explicitly: 

# rsync example
rsync -a --exclude='.env*' ./ user@host:/var/www/site/

3. No real environment variables set on the production process

Most hosting platforms — a PaaS dashboard, a container orchestrator's secret store, a systemd unit's Environment= directives — let you set environment variables directly on the running process, with no file on disk at all. Relying on always having a correctly-placed .env file in every environment is both more fragile and strictly riskier than this.

4. No server rule blocking dotfiles as a second layer

Defense in depth: even with the deploy step fixed, a server or CDN rule that denies any request for a dotfile means a stray copy — a one-off manual deploy, a misconfigured mirror — is not actually reachable. 

# nginx example
location ~ /\.env { deny all; return 404; }

# Apache example (.htaccess in the document root)
<Files ~ "^\.env">
  Require all denied
</Files>

If this checker already found an exposure

Fix the deploy cause first (steps 1–3 above), then treat every value that file held as compromised and rotate it immediately — an API key, a database password, a session secret, a third-party token. Rotation is the only remedy once a credential has been served publicly, even once: there is no way to know for certain it was not already fetched by an automated scanner before you found it.

Run the Dotenv Exposure Checker against your production URL to see which of these, if any, apply to your deployment right now. Only run it against a site you own or are authorised to test.
